In recognition of its progress during 2025, ICON achieved an EcoVadis score of 87/100, earning Platinum Medal status and ranking ICON in the top 1% of all organisations assessed, while also improving its CDP Climate Change score from B- to B. ICON was also named among TIME World’s Most Sustainable Companies. On publication of the report, ICON’s Chief Executive Officer, Barry Balfe, commented: "During 2025, we continued to modernise our services, embrace new technologies and strengthen the capabilities of our people to help bring life-enhancing treatments to patients faster. The achievements highlighted in this report reflect the dedication of our teams around the world and the positive impact we can make when we combine scientific expertise, technology and a strong commitment to deliver for our customers." Highlights include: Renewable electricity: 97.05% of global electricity consumption in 2025 was from renewable sources. Energy reduction: 24% reduction in kWh of electricity compared to 2018 baseline, surpassing the company's 2030 target of a 20% reduction ahead of schedule. Emissions reductions: ICON achieved a 73.56% reduction in Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions compared to the 2019 baseline, exceeding its near-term SBTi target. The company also reported a 6.74% reduction in Scope 3 emissions compared to 2022. Sustainable Procurement program: By the end of 2025, 94% of preferred suppliers had sustainability engagement plans and 79% had an EcoVadis scorecard. Advancing health equity and patient access In 2025, ICON supported over 1,370 clinical studies involving more than 411,400 patients, through data-driven solutions and patient-centred services. These efforts contributed to 25 unique products receiving original or supplemental approval. The company also strengthened partnerships across the healthcare ecosystem to support more representative and accessible clinical research. Leveraging innovation and AI to accelerate progress ICON continued to invest in AI-enabled solutions designed to support clinical development and operational excellence. ICON’s proprietary Orbis platform received the AI Project of the Year award at the Analytics & AI Awards 2025, as the company continued to deploy AI capabilities across clinical trial operations, helping teams work more efficiently, improving decision-making and accelerating delivery for customers, with robust governance and human oversight. Fostering a culture of inclusion and belonging ICON continued to prioritise employee development, engagement and wellbeing across its global workforce who highlighted ICON's collaborative environment, flexible working practices and strong colleague relationships as key strengths of the organisation in company surveys. The company was also recognised as one of TIME World's Best Companies, Forbes World’s Top Companies for Women and America’s Best Employers for Company Culture 2025. The company's corporate giving program has now funded over 135 charities since its launch, with employees participating in community initiatives around the world through volunteering, fundraising and corporate giving programs. Furthermore, ICON expanded its global partnership with UNICEF to support humanitarian relief efforts and health initiatives worldwide. The full ICON Cares 2025 ESG Report is available here . From molecule to medicine, we deliver integrated consulting, clinical development, commercialisation and post-marketing solutions to pharmaceutical, biotechnology, medical device, government and public health organisations worldwide. articles.summary: Have you ever used a conditioner that someone swears by, only to wonder if you accidentally bought the wrong bottle? Their hair is soft, smooth, and shiny. Yours feels flat, greasy, dry, coated, or somehow looks no different. Chances are, the conditioner is not the problem. The same formula can perform differently because hair care isn't one-size-fits-all. Your hair type, strand thickness, density, condition, damage, and the way you apply products can all influence the result. And to understand why, lets breakdown what conditioner is actually designed to do. The Science of How Conditioner Works Hair naturally carries an electrical charge, and that charge can become more pronounced when the hair surface is weathered or damaged. Heat styling, chemical treatments, friction, and changes to the hair's protective surface can all affect how the fiber behaves. The hair cuticle affects electrical charge based on how flat or damaged its scales are. Healthy cuticles keep a neutral or slightly negative charge, while damaged cuticles create a strong negative charge that causes static and frizz. Conditioners use the law of electrical attraction to fix hair damage by matching positive charges in the product to the negative charges on the hair cuticle. Conditioners contain positively charged ingredients called cationic conditioning agents, which are attracted to negatively charged areas of the hair fiber. These ingredients deposit onto the hair surface to help reduce static and friction, improve slip, and leave hair feeling smoother and easier to manage. But conditioning isn't one-size-fits-all. Different hair structures distribute natural oils differently. Fine hair can become weighed down more easily than thicker hair. Damaged areas may behave differently from healthier sections of the very same strand. A curl pattern changes the way hair bends, tangles, retains its shape, and experiences dryness along its length. That's why two people can use the exact same conditioner and have completely different results. Hair type is one part of the picture. Strand thickness, density, porosity, damage, treatment history, and product application add another layer to what your hair needs. The formula isn't the only thing that matters. How you apply conditioner matters, too. Putting a blob of conditioner on your scalp is not setting you up for clean-looking hair. You also have different types of conditioners that have different application techniques: Rinse-out conditioners, hair masks, and leave-in treatments are designed to do different jobs. Using the right product in the wrong way can make even a great product feel too heavy on your hair. Why Hair Type Matters The difference between straight, wavy, curly, and coily hair comes down primarily to the visible geometry of the hair fiber. That geometry influences how hair behaves, how easily natural scalp oils can travel along the strand, where friction occurs, and how much conditioning support the lengths may need. Hair type is not a complete diagnosis. Two people with curly hair can have completely different strand thicknesses, densities, levels of damage, and conditioning needs. The same is true for every hair type. Think of hair type as the starting point, not the final answer. Straight Hair Straight hair has little to no natural bend along the fiber, creating a relatively direct path from scalp to ends. That can allow natural scalp oils to travel more easily along the hair shaft than they do through highly curved or tightly coiled hair. It can also mean that some straight hair becomes oily or weighed down more quickly, particularly when conditioner is applied heavily near the roots. For fine or low-density straight hair especially, a heavy conditioning routine can leave strands looking flat rather than healthy. The Straight Hair Conditioner, formulated with avocado oil, is designed to condition and smooth without unnecessary heaviness. Apply it primarily from the mid-lengths through the ends, especially if your roots tend to become oily, and rinse thoroughly. For deeper conditioning, swap in the Straight Hair Mask once a week. Its seaweed extract helps support a smooth-looking hair surface and reflective shine. Leave it on for 5 to 10 minutes before rinsing. A lightweight leave-in can also be useful for dry or damaged ends. The key is to use only what your hair needs. Fine straight hair often benefits more from strategic conditioning than from layering multiple heavy products. Wavy Hair Wavy hair can have competing needs along the same length. Roots may become oily or experience buildup, while the bends and curves through the mid-lengths and ends can feel drier, frizzier, or less defined. Add variation in strand thickness and density, and one conditioning strategy won't work for everyone. The solution isn't necessarily a heavier conditioner. The solution might include adding moisturizing products to your routine. The Wavy Hair Conditioner, formulated with argan oil, can be applied from around ear level through the ends, concentrating on the areas that need the most conditioning and keeping the product away from the scalp if your roots tend to become oily. For deeper conditioning, replace your regular conditioner with the Wavy Hair Mask once or twice a week. Its vegan squalane formula provides additional conditioning support without requiring you to overload the hair every wash day. Leave it on for 5 to 10 minutes before rinsing. The Wavy Leave-In Treatment can help support softness and manageability between washes, especially through dry or damaged lengths. The goal is to moisturize and condition the lengths without automatically assuming that every wash requires the same level of conditioning. Curly Hair Curly hair's bends, loops, and spirals can make it more difficult for natural scalp oils to travel evenly from the roots to the ends. As a result, the lengths can be more prone to dryness, tangling, and friction. Curly hair can also experience mechanical stress at the points where the strand bends. Damage, porosity, strand thickness, and styling habits will all influence how much conditioning support an individual routine needs. The Curly Hair Conditioner, formulated with Jamaican black castor oil and hemp seed protein, is designed to provide conditioning and slip while supporting detangling. Apply it generously through the lengths and use your fingers or a wide-tooth comb to gently work through tangles while the conditioner is in the hair. Let it sit for a few minutes before rinsing. For additional conditioning, use the Custom SOS Curly Hair Mask in place of conditioner once or twice a week and leave it on for around 10 minutes. For best results, follow with the Curly Leave-In Treatment on damp hair. This creates an additional conditioning layer that can support softness, manageability, and reduced friction as the hair dries. For styling, apply Super Shape Curl Cream to wet hair to help define your natural curl pattern while maintaining flexibility. For curly hair, conditioning isn't simply about adding more of the same product; it's layering in moisture products and applying a mask regularly. Coily Hair The main thing to keep in mind when caring for coily hair is consistent conditioning. Coily hair's tight bends and curves can make it more difficult for natural oils from the scalp to travel evenly through the lengths, which is why the hair can be more prone to dryness, tangling, and breakage. Start with a Coily Hair Shampoo that cleanses the scalp and hair without leaving the lengths feeling overly stripped. Follow with a Coily Hair Conditioner to help provide slip, softness, and easier detangling. Work the conditioner through the mid-lengths and ends, taking time to gently distribute it through the hair before rinsing. For additional conditioning support, swap your regular conditioner for a Coily Hair Mask once or twice a week. This gives your hair a more intensive conditioning treatment and can help support softness and manageability. Leave the mask on for 5 to 10 minutes before rinsing, then adjust the frequency based on how your hair responds. The goal isn't to use the most products or the richest formula. It's to create a routine that works with your hair's structure and gives your strands the cleansing and conditioning support they need. Do You Wonder How You Use Your Conditioner? Finding the right conditioner is only part of the equation. How you apply it and rinse it can change the result. Your scalp and your lengths don't necessarily have the same needs. Your scalp naturally produces sebum, while the mid-lengths and ends are farther from the source of those natural oils. For many people, concentrating conditioner through the lengths and ends, rather than applying it heavily at the roots, can help provide conditioning where it's needed without leaving the scalp area feeling weighed down. If your roots regularly feel oily or flat after wash day while your ends still feel dry, the formula may not be the only thing to reconsider. You may simply need to adjust where you're applying your conditioner, how much you're using, or how thoroughly you're rinsing. Why Rinsing Your Conditioner Properly Matters Rinsing is where your conditioning routine comes together. Too little rinsing can leave excess product behind, causing hair to feel heavy, coated, or greasy. But rinsing until your hair feels completely stripped isn't the goal either. Start with comfortably lukewarm water and allow it to flow through the lengths of your hair, helping to remove excess product. Avoid excessively hot water, which can leave the hair and scalp feeling dry or uncomfortable. If you enjoy finishing with cooler water, you can, but what matters most is using a comfortable temperature and rinsing thoroughly enough for your hair and the amount of product you've used. As you rinse, gently guide your hair downward with your fingers, following the natural direction of the strands. There's no need to scrub, bunch, or aggressively move the hair around. Instead, let the water do most of the work while you gently separate the lengths and help rinse away excess conditioner. This can be particularly helpful for hair that is prone to tangling, including curly and coily textures. Use the feel of your hair and your hair type as your guide. Continue rinsing until it no longer feels heavily coated but still feels soft and manageable. Straight hair looks and feels cleaner if all of the conditioner is thoroughly rinsed. For curly and coily hair, your goal isn't to remove every trace of conditioning from the hair. The goal isn't to use the richest conditioner or the most products. It's to understand how your hair type behaves, then build a conditioning routine around it. Better hair days start with a Function hair type routine.

articles.summary: By Fred Greenberg, Director of Engineering Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) and Linear Pluggable Optics (LPO) address different layers of AI optical interconnects. While CPO maximizes bandwidth density, LPO balances power, cost, and deployability. What Is Co-Packaged Optics (CPO)? CPO places optical engines in close physical proximity to the switch ASIC, typically within the same package or PCB substrate. The Mechanism: Shortening the electrical interconnect between the switch SerDes and the optical interface dramatically reduces signal loss. This eliminates the need for power-hungry signal conditioning. The Challenge: Tight coupling between the optics and the switch ASIC complicates manufacturing, testing, and thermal management. What Is Linear Pluggable Optics (LPO)? LPO takes an evolutionary approach. Instead of redesigning the system architecture, it simplifies the optical module itself by removing the Digital Signal Processor (DSP). The Mechanism: The design uses linear driver and transimpedance amplifier (TIA) components, shifting signal compensation entirely to the host switch ASIC. The Benefit: Eliminating the DSP significantly reduces module power consumption and Bill of Materials (BOM) costs, especially in short-reach applications. The Form Factor: LPO retains standard pluggable form factors like QSFP-DD. This allows integrators to deploy modules in existing switch platforms while preserving hot-swap ability, established operational workflows, and vendor interoperability. At OSS, we are dedicated to breaking performance barriers. We are actively exploring and integrating breakthrough technologies like LPO to help our customers build cooler, faster, and more cost-effective AI environments.
